clue.text: One sometimes does before shaving–with heavy exercise, too.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: brushing soap into foam on the face before a shave
second meaning: what a hard-worked horse or athlete does, sweating into a froth

explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across two lights, 1 and 5. 'too' tells you the same phrase also covers the sweaty sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom covers both foaming shaving soap and getting into a sweat from effort, literally or figuratively.

clue.text: The home of the brave?

parts.note: the patriotic phrase from the US anthem, reread with brave as a Native American warrior

explanation.walkthrough: The line suggests America in the anthem; the question mark says to read 'brave' as the old word for a Native American warrior, whose dwelling is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A domed tent dwelling of some Native American peoples, so literally a warrior's lodging.

clue.text: Like some equilateral parallelograms.

parts.note: a near-literal geometric description: a parallelogram with four equal sides has a particular named shape

explanation.walkthrough: There is no hidden trick here: a parallelogram with all sides equal is a rhombus, and the adjective follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhombus is an equilateral parallelogram, and the adjective form describes such a diamond shape.

clue.text: Perhaps the actress who could beat the hide off you!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Cornelia Otis ..., the American actress and writer

definitions.text: who could beat the hide off you
definitions.meaning: second meaning: one who strips the pelt from animals

explanation.walkthrough: Cornelia Otis Skinner was a well-known American stage actress and monologist; the second half is a literal flayer of hides.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of a famous actress is also the trade name for someone who removes animal pelts.

clue.text: What's washed up on the shore forever might go to her head.

definitions.text: What's washed up on the shore forever might go to her head.

parts.words: What's washed up on the shore forever might go to her head.
parts.note: a breaker that never stops is an everlasting surge of sea, and the same phrase is a lasting hair curl

explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, the phrase is a sea wave that lasts for ever; in the salon it is the chemically set curl, the perm, that goes on a woman's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairstyle of chemically set curls that lasts for months, known for short as a perm.

clue.text: See 1
To tell the truth, he never did!

definitions.text: To tell the truth, he never did!

parts.words: To tell the truth, he never did!
parts.note: the biblical man struck dead for lying to the apostles, whose name became a byword for a liar

explanation.walkthrough: In Acts 5 this man lied about the price of his land and fell dead; 'an Ananias' is an old term for a liar.
explanation.definitionFit: A biblical figure famous for deceit, so his name stands for a habitual liar.

clue.text: Typified by Uriah with a star performance having a close-fitting sound.

parts.note: a hit is a smash success, a performance that makes someone a star

indicators.note: sound tells you to take a word as it is spoken, not as it is spelt

parts.note: close-fitting clothes are tight

explanation.surface: Someone like Uriah Heep putting on a starring turn in snug clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: Uriah makes you think of Dickens's Heep, but the Bible's Uriah the Hittite is meant. 'sound' says TIGHT is heard, so it is written TITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Uriah, husband of Bathsheba, is called the Hittite in the Bible, so he is the example of that people.

clue.text: E. in a state of undress displays impolite behavior.

indicators.note: a state of disorder: the letters of the following words are thrown into a new arrangement

parts.note: the letter E as written
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'a state of undress' looks like nakedness, but 'in a state of' is the signal: E plus UNDRESS is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Rudeness is a lack of courtesy, the quality of behaving without manners.

clue.text: More silly than sweet, sticky stuff on fire, sort of.

parts.note: goo is any sticky, gooey substance, often sugary

indicators.note: sort of says the letters of the word fire are only approximately that word, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet, sticky stuff on fire' reads as burning syrup, but 'on' only joins the pieces, and 'sort of' is the shuffle signal, not a hedge: it makes FIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Goofy means silly or daft, and this is its comparative.

clue.text: Began like the actor Little Edward.

parts.note: the star of a show is its leading actor
Ted is the short, familiar form of Edward

explanation.surface: Getting going like an actor called Little Edward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Edward' looks like the name of a child actor, but 'little' asks for the short pet form of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Started is a simple synonym of began, both meaning commenced.

clue.text: Suggests the part of the athlete that might get out of joint really defines good behavior on his part.

definitions.text: the part of the athlete that might get out of joint
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read as two words: a sports star's hip joint, which can be dislocated
second meaning: fair and generous conduct in competition

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as SPORTSMAN'S HIP for the joint that may dislocate; whole, it is fair play. 'Suggests' and 'really defines' tie the two readings together.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsmanship is graceful, fair conduct expected of competitors, win or lose.

clue.text: Forbid its existence inter alia for this country.

indicators.note: inter is Latin for among or between, so the banned word goes inside the next word

parts.note: taken as written
to forbid something's existence is to ban it

explanation.surface: A country that bans things among others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inter alia' looks like the Latin tag for 'among other things', but here 'inter' alone is the signal, Latin for between.
explanation.definitionFit: Albania is a Balkan nation on the Adriatic coast.

clue.text: That's what you think!

parts.note: a dismissive retort, reread literally as describing a personal view

explanation.walkthrough: The retort usually means 'you are wrong'; taken literally, what you think is your view.
explanation.definitionFit: An opinion is a belief or judgement held by a person, literally what they think.

clue.text: What the electric company has in its favor.

definitions.text: What the electric company has in its favor.

parts.words: What the electric company has in its favor.
parts.note: accounting term for short-term holdings, punning on the flow an electricity supplier sells

explanation.walkthrough: In accounts, these are holdings like cash and stock; an electricity firm's stock in trade is literally electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Short-term business holdings on a balance sheet, with a pun on electrical flow.

clue.text: Take advantage of someone and offer him an apple, perhaps–but you should treat the villain with it.

definitions.text: you should treat the villain with it

parts.note: to con someone is to swindle or dupe them
as Eve tempted Adam with the fruit in Eden, offering an apple is an example of tempting

explanation.surface: Fleece a man and lure him with fruit, though a scoundrel deserves something worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The Eden story makes the apple the classic temptation, hence 'perhaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: Contempt is scorn, the attitude a villain earns from decent people.

clue.text: Guesses a bit high?

parts.note: a near-literal description of reckoning too large a figure

explanation.walkthrough: Guessing high is overshooting a figure, which is the verb in its third-person form.
explanation.definitionFit: To overestimate is to judge an amount too large, so the guess comes out too high.

clue.text: Eastern title that makes the point very loud to finish one.

parts.note: E is east, one of the compass points
ff is fortissimo, the musical mark for very loud
to end is to finish
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A title from the East, declared at full volume at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Effendi is a Turkish honorific for a man of standing, like sir.

clue.text: Looks over what came from mine, but doesn't look very well.

definitions.note: the clue gives a description of the thing (a verb phrase), the answer is the thing itself, a noun

parts.note: to eye something is to look it over
ore is the rock dug from a mine

explanation.surface: Someone inspects what came out of their mine, which looks poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' looks like the possessive but is the pit.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyesore is something ugly, a thing that is unpleasant to see.

clue.text: English caricaturist putting a number on the broken line.

parts.note: ten is a number

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of line are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cartoonist adding a figure to a dashed line.
explanation.walkthrough: A broken line in drawing is a dashed one, which suits a caricaturist; here 'broken' is the shuffle signal, giving NIEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Tenniel drew cartoons for Punch and illustrated Alice in Wonderland.

clue.text: Possibly a lizard or a crocodile, as it comes up to the old city in around a final part.

definitions.text: Possibly a lizard or a crocodile

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means the word as is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: taken as written
Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

indicators.note: around says the letters of in surround the following letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A reptile reaching an ancient city near the end of a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes up' gives SA because this is a down entry, read bottom to top. 'around a' gives IAN, the 'final part' of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Saurian describes lizards and similar reptiles; a crocodile was once grouped with them.

clue.text: You might spare the spare with the one with his hand out, or alter the definition.

definitions.text: You might spare the spare with the one with his hand out
definitions.meaning: first meaning: loose coins, the spare kind given to a beggar

explanation.walkthrough: Spare change is small coins handed to someone begging; 'or alter the definition' winks that the word also means alter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both small coins and the verb to make different, an ordinary double sense.

clue.text: A stout return with an uncertain fate, which proves material.

indicators.note: a return goes back, so the word for stout is written backwards

parts.note: stout means fat

indicators.note: an uncertain fate is unsettled, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fat man coming back to an unknown destiny, which proves to be a matter of cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns FAT into TAF; 'uncertain' turns FATE into FETA.
explanation.definitionFit: Taffeta is a crisp, lustrous fabric, often silk, used for gowns.

clue.text: Peerless description of the Frenchman's negative view on a sort of it.

parts.note: non is French for no
such means of that kind, a sort of the thing mentioned

explanation.surface: A Frenchman says no to some view, describing something matchless.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonsuch is a person or thing without equal, a paragon, so the word describes the peerless.

clue.text: You might see a worker tip his lid and come out of it.

definitions.text: You might see a worker tip his lid and come out of it.

parts.words: You might see a worker tip his lid and come out of it.
parts.note: tipping a lid sounds like raising a hat, but here it is lifting a street cover

explanation.walkthrough: 'tip his lid' suggests a polite hat-raise; the lid is the iron cover a utility worker lifts to climb out.
explanation.definitionFit: A manhole is the covered opening in a street through which workers reach drains and cables.

clue.text: A southern republican puts one in a hat with John in Glasgow.

indicators.note: puts and in together say that one letter is placed within another word
in, with puts, says the letter goes inside the hat

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
Ian is the Scottish form of John

explanation.surface: A southern Republican tucks something into a hat, with a Scottish friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puts' and 'in' place I inside HAT for HAIT. 'republican' with a small r means a citizen of a republic, not a party member: Haiti is a Caribbean republic south of the US.
explanation.definitionFit: A Haitian belongs to the Republic of Haiti, which lies south of the United States.

clue.text: Comparatively right, according to some. (Fasten firmly on the junction!)

indicators.note: in an across clue, putting the fixing word on the junction means it follows the junction's letter

parts.note: a T-junction is a road meeting shaped like the letter T
to rivet is to fix firmly with metal pins

explanation.surface: A puzzling claim about relative correctness, then a fixing instruction at a crossroads.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition rests on the old British simile 'as right as a trivet', meaning perfectly fine; a trivet is a three-legged stand for a pot.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom compares soundness to a trivet, so in that saying the object is the standard of being all right.

clue.text: An awful lot with it, but nothing goes up wrong with the end of silence.

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for great wealth, a lot of riches

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing

indicators.note: the word up goes the wrong way round, so it is read backwards
the end of a word is its latter part, so the opening letters of silence are dropped

explanation.surface: Lots of goods and trendiness, yet nothing rises properly once the quiet ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' sends UP the wrong way to give PU, and 'the end of' takes only the closing LENCE of SILENCE, dropping its opening SI. 'with it, but' and 'goes' are linking padding in this loose old-style clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulence is great wealth and lavish abundance, a huge amount of riches.
